Like the KEK structure design, the SLAC design utilizes a series of linear welds to join the structure halves together, as shown in Figure 5-center. Attaching the vacuum flanges is more complex, as it requires a separate setup for the radial welds of the beam port flanges as well as XY CNC-controlled plug welds of the side- mounted vacuum pumping ports. Because the electron beam must “see” the weld joint, the vacuum flanges Page 5 of 55 “Manufacturing full-scale high gradient copper accelerators: Electron beam welding and allied processes” Prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy ARDAP program need to be welded onto the stems after joining the stem to the body, otherwise the flange will shadow the weld joint. These additional welds require multiple pump down cycles and setups, incurring significant costs and increasing the likelihood of structure contamination with vacuum pump hydrocarbons or weld vapor. Furthermore, the four waveguide WR90 vacuum flanges are mechanically fastened to the AS body. The technical feasibility of this approach is unknown, as the waveguide stainless steel bolts must fasten into the AS, potentially causing deformation of the delicate internal copper RF structure. Also, the reliability of the copper knife edge to annealed copper gasket to stainless steel knife edge vacuum seal is unknown. Additional design compromises of this SLAC structure include clamp-on cooling circuits and push-only tuning pins. Weld joint design and process development is also not extensively discussed, although insufficient weld penetration create a risk for virtual vacuum leaks formed by two tightly pressed surfaces, while over powering the welds can result in spatter on the inside RF surface. Although not optimized, both SLAC and KEK EBW welded structure design address two fundamental challenge of welding compared to brazing: the beam must be able to ‘see’ the weld joint and welded joints must be formed serially. Risk for virtual vacuum leaks between two pressed surfaces are also a challenge for welded NCRF structures, limiting potential design choices compared brazed NCFC components. A.4 Baseline RF & Mechanical design While a complete mature design for welded, split-cell NCRF accelerating structures has yet to be demonstrated; we will utilize a C-band, quadrant type, distributed-coupling cell stack proposed as part of the C3 initiative [9]. The C3 concept utilizes liquid nitrogen cooling of conventional copper to improve surface conductivity, and thus increase the structure shut impedance by nearly a factor of 3 [10]. In its current baseline design reiteration, the C3 accelerating structure is 1.1m long device composed of 4 quadrants and contains x40 RF cells with re-entrant nose-cone type features.
